walkthroughs.body_html:
In GCSE Physics, we model light as straight-line rays.

An arrow on a line shows which way light is travelling. Light always goes in straight lines until something makes it change direction.

That's it for the model — simple but powerful. ✨

When a ray hits a surface, draw a dashed line at 90° to the surface at the point of contact. That dashed line is the normal.

Every angle in optics is measured from the normal, never from the surface itself. This trips up a lot of students — don't be one of them!

For a flat mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. Both measured from the normal.

This neat, mirror-like reflection is called specular reflection. A rough surface scatters light in all directions instead — that's called diffuse reflection.

mcqs.q: Angles in optics are measured from which line?
options: The mirror surface
The normal
The horizontal
The incoming ray itself

mcqs.q: If a ray hits a flat mirror with an angle of incidence of 40°, what is the angle of reflection?
How do you see a non-luminous object like a book?
options: The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
Light from a source reflects off the book and enters your eyes.
The book emits a special invisible signal that your brain detects directly.
Your eyes send out beams of vision that hit the book and let you see it.

mcqs.q: If one EM wave has a higher frequency than another, what is true about its wavelength?
options: The book emits a special invisible signal that your brain detects directly.
It is also longer, because both increase together.
It is shorter — wavelength and frequency are inversely related (c = f x lambda).
It is unchanged — only the speed differs.

mcqs.q: When you push a wall, what does Newton's third law say about the wall?
options: The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
The wall only pushes back if your force is strong enough to make it react.
It is unchanged — only the speed differs.
The wall exerts an equal and opposite force on you at the same instant.
